records.why: The old sentence suggested the power-of-a-power law always goes before the product and quotient laws, which is false: in (2³ × 2⁴)² the product comes first. The true rule is 'innermost brackets first'. Checked: (2³ × 2⁴)² = (2⁷)² = 2¹⁴, where the product law is used first.
records.old: The Power-of-a-Power Law must be resolved before the Product or Quotient Law when it appears inside brackets.
records.new: Work from the inside of the brackets outwards: in P3 and P4 the power-of-a-power sits inside the brackets, so it is simplified first.
records.group_headline: The rule 'power of a power is always done first' was overstated; the correct rule is brackets first, working from the inside out
records.reference: Standard order of operations (BODMAS/brackets first); KICD Grade 10 Mathematics, Indices

records.why: Same correction as Lesson 6.
records.old: The bracket comes first because the power-of-a-power law must be resolved before the product or quotient law can combine the powers into a single base and index.
records.new: The bracket comes first because brackets are worked from the inside outwards: (2³)² sits inside the bracket, so it must become a single power of 2 before the product and quotient laws can combine the powers.

records.why: The old Problem Set 3 was scientifically wrong and not teachable yet: VO₂ max falls at altitude (it is not 'scaled by a factor of 1'), VO₂ max is not a race speed ('fastest runner'), and part (iii) needed negative indices (6.4 × 10¹ mL = 6.4 × 10⁻² L), which this sub-strand does not teach. The new set uses training distance, which needs only the four laws. Checked: 10⁴ × 10² = 10⁶ m; 10⁶ m ÷ 10³ = 10³ km = 1,000 km; 2⁶ × (2²)² = 2⁶ × 2⁴ = 2¹⁰ = 1,024 km; 10³ ÷ 10³ = 10⁰ = 1. Teacher to decide: whether training-distance figures feel right for your learners, or whether you prefer another athletics context; the science (altitude lowers VO₂ max) is the reason for the change.
records.old: • PROBLEM SET 3 — Eldoret Athletics Performance (Groups E & F): A sports scientist in Eldoret records a baseline VO₂ max score for a runner as 6.4 × 10¹ mL/kg/min. At altitude, performance data is scaled by a factor of (10¹)⁰. (i) Apply the zero-index rule to simplify the scaling factor and explain in words what it means for the measurement. (ii) The scientist compares three runners whose scores are 6.4 × 10¹, 3.2 × 10¹, and 1.6 × 10¹. Express the ratio of the fastest to the slowest score using the quotient law. (iii) If the scientist wants to express her data in units of 10³ mL/kg/min (i.e., per litre per kg per min), rewrite 6.4 × 10¹ accordingly and state the new coefficient.
records.new: • PROBLEM SET 3 — Eldoret Athletics Training (Groups E & F): A training camp near Eldoret records the work of its distance runners. (i) A runner covers 10⁴ m in one session and completes 10² sessions in a season. Use the product law to find the season's distance in metres as a single power of 10, then use the quotient law to change it to kilometres (10⁶ ÷ 10³). (ii) The camp has 2⁶ athletes and in one training block each runs (2²)² km. Use the power-of-a-power law and then the product law to find the camp's total distance in km as a single power of 2, and evaluate it. (iii) Two runners each log 10³ km in a season. Use the quotient law to write the ratio of their distances, 10³ ÷ 10³, as a power of 10, and explain in words what the answer means.
records.group_headline: Lesson 7's Eldoret altitude problem was scientifically wrong (altitude lowers VO₂ max, it does not leave it unchanged) and needed negative indices not yet taught; replaced by a training-distance problem (and the same thread fixed in the unit overview)
records.reference: Wilber, R. L. (2004) Altitude Training and Athletic Performance, Human Kinetics; US Standard Atmosphere 1976 (pressure at Eldoret about 2,100 m is about 77% of sea level)

records.why: The formula 'air pressure = 10^(−0.15 × altitude in km)' is invented and wrong: it gives 10^(−0.36) = 0.44 atm at 2.4 km, but the standard atmosphere gives about 0.75 atm at 2,400 m. Also Eldoret is about 2,100 m (Iten is about 2,400 m), and a decimal exponent is not a use of whole-number indices. Standard atmosphere check: P/P₀ = (1 − 2.25577×10⁻⁵ × h)^5.25588 gives 0.775 at 2,100 m and 0.746 at 2,400 m. The new bullet uses a camp-distance calculation that uses the product law: 2⁶ × 2⁴ = 2¹⁰ = 1,024 km.
records.old: • Rift Valley long-distance athletes train at altitudes where air pressure is approximately 10^(−0.15 × altitude_in_km) atmospheres. Learners observe that a runner's "altitude exponent" at 2.4 km (Eldoret) is a decimal power, bridging their understanding of whole-number indices toward later work on rational exponents.
records.new: • Rift Valley long-distance athletes train at Eldoret and Iten, about 2,100 to 2,400 m above sea level, where air pressure is roughly three-quarters of the sea-level value. Learners total a training camp's work with the index laws: 2⁶ athletes each running (2²)² km in a training block cover 2⁶ × 2⁴ = 2¹⁰ = 1,024 km altogether.
records.reference: US Standard Atmosphere 1976 (NOAA/NASA/USAF); Wilber, R. L. (2004) Altitude Training and Athletic Performance, Human Kinetics

records.why: Old Problem Set 1 told learners to 'round to the nearest power' (both figures round to 10¹², so the ratio would be 10⁰ = 1, which is meaningless) and then grew the budget 100-fold. The new set keeps the quotient law but divides the powers of ten and the coefficients: 10¹² ÷ 10¹¹ = 10; 3.7 ÷ 5.9 ≈ 0.63; 0.63 × 10 ≈ 6.3 times; and 5.9 × 10¹¹ ÷ 10⁴ = 5.9 × 10⁷. Both calculations rechecked.
records.old: • PROBLEM SET 1 — National Budget (Groups A & B): Kenya's 2023/24 national budget was approximately KSh 3.7 × 10¹². The education sector received approximately KSh 5.9 × 10¹¹. (i) Express the total budget and the education allocation each as a single power of 10 (round to nearest power). (ii) Using the quotient law, calculate the ratio of the total budget to the education allocation. Express your answer in index form and as an ordinary number. (iii) If next year's budget grows by a factor of 10², what will the new budget be in standard form?
records.new: • PROBLEM SET 1 — National Budget (Groups A & B): Kenya's 2023/24 national budget was approximately KSh 3.7 × 10¹². The education sector received approximately KSh 5.9 × 10¹¹. (i) Write down the power of 10 in each figure. (ii) Use the quotient law on the powers of 10 to work out 10¹² ÷ 10¹¹, then divide the coefficients (3.7 ÷ 5.9, to 2 decimal places) and combine them to find roughly how many times larger the budget is than the education allocation. (iii) Suppose the education allocation is shared equally among 10⁴ schools. Use the quotient law to find each school's share in standard form.
records.group_headline: Lesson 7 budget problem was unsolvable as written (both amounts round to 10¹²) and the exit card mixed 4 × 10¹² and 3.7 × 10¹²; rewritten with consistent figures and checked answers

records.why: Problem Set 2 told learners to use the product law on 3² × 2¹⁰ (different bases, so the law cannot be used) while the teacher notes warned against exactly that. The lab now has 2⁴ computers so the product law applies: 2⁴ × 2¹⁰ = 2¹⁴ = 16,384 GB; server ratio 2¹⁵ ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2⁵ = 32; (2³)² × 2⁷ = 2⁶ × 2⁷ = 2¹³ = 8,192 GB. The USB part was also ambiguous ('a stack of (2⁷)² sticks').
records.old: • PROBLEM SET 2 — ICT Lab Data Storage (Groups C & D): Mwangi Secondary School, Nairobi, is equipping an ICT lab. Each of the 3² computers has a hard drive of 2¹⁰ gigabytes. (i) Use the product law to find the total storage in the lab. Express your answer as a single index expression and in ordinary form. (ii) The school server holds 2¹⁵ GB. Using the quotient law, find how many times larger the server is than one computer's hard drive. (iii) A USB stick holds 2⁷ GB. Using the power-of-a-power law, find the capacity (in GB) of a stack of (2⁷)² such sticks.
records.new: • PROBLEM SET 2 — ICT Lab Data Storage (Groups C & D): Mwangi Secondary School, Nairobi, is equipping an ICT lab. Each of the 2⁴ computers has a hard drive of 2¹⁰ gigabytes. (i) Use the product law to find the total storage in the lab. Express your answer as a single index expression and in ordinary form. (ii) The school server holds 2¹⁵ GB. Using the quotient law, find how many times larger the server is than one computer's hard drive. (iii) A shop stocks (2³)² USB sticks of 2⁷ GB each. Using the power-of-a-power law and then the product law, find their total capacity in GB.
records.group_headline: Lesson 7 ICT problem asked learners to use the product law on different bases (3² × 2¹⁰), which is not allowed; rewritten so every part works

records.why: Misconception note rewritten to match the new Problem Set 2; expected answer 2¹⁴.
records.old: Anticipated misconception A (Product Set 2): learners multiply 3² × 2¹⁰ by adding exponents despite different bases. Say: 'Pause — which law allows you to add exponents? Does that law require the bases to be the same or different? Look back at your notes.'
records.new: Anticipated misconception A (Problem Set 2): learners write 2⁴ × 2¹⁰ = 4¹⁴ (they multiply the bases as well as adding the indices). Say: 'Pause — expand 2² × 2³ to check. How many 2s are there altogether? Does the base change when we multiply powers with the same base?' (A useful contrast: 3² × 2¹⁰ cannot be combined, because the bases differ.)

records.why: Guideline 7: Reasoning is the science (here mathematical) idea that links evidence to claim. The old text called the 'So What?' sentence the reasoning, and called the working 'index-law working' (mixing evidence and reasoning). The named law is the reasoning.

records.new: each group's poster is structured as a claim (the computed result), evidence (the numbers and step-by-step working from the data), and reasoning (the index law named in the margin, which explains why each step is allowed); the 'So What?' sentence then links the result back to the driving question.

records.old: Examples include: (L1) the census card 47,564,296 ≈ 4.8 × 10⁷; (L2) the maize-grain expansion 2³ × 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁷; (L3) the Kericho tea-farm product-law example; (L4) the yield ratio 3⁵ ÷ 3² = 3³ and the zero-index result from equal-base division 5³ ÷ 5³ = 5⁰ = 1; (L5) Kenya's national debt written as (10³)² = 10⁶; (L6) a multi-step computation combining all four laws; (L7) a combined-law simplification problem using Kenyan population data.

records.why: The driving question promises 'huge or tiny quantities', but nothing in Lessons 1 to 8 teaches negative indices (Lesson 1 says not to introduce them; the laws are for whole-number indices). Several lessons implied they would come (Lesson 5 'fractional and negative indices in Lessons 7–8', Lesson 6 'very small numbers ... Lesson 7', Lesson 7 'explored negative and fractional indices', Lesson 8 task with 0.000008 m). This group makes the plan consistent: the unit covers whole-number indices and says openly that tiny numbers are left for later. 'Grade 11 territory' was also unverified. Teacher to decide: keep it as parked, or add a short negative-index lesson (a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ) because the driving question names tiny quantities.
records.old: The pink notes about fractional indices and logarithms — those are Grade 11 territory.'
records.new: Pink notes about negative indices (the 'tiny' half of our driving question, for example a maize grain of 0.0003 kg), fractional indices and logarithms are for later study. We have answered the huge-number half of our question and left the tiny-number half open, and that is honest.'

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly names base and index, expands powers as repeated multiplication with correct values, and clearly explains why Card B is more compact and less error-prone than Card A.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Names base and index and expands correctly, with only a brief or partial explanation of why index form is compact.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses base and index, or expands incorrectly, or gives no explanation of the compact form.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Applies the product, quotient, zero-index and power-of-a-power laws correctly in every part, including the multi-step problems, with the right order of steps and correct final values.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Applies most laws correctly with minor slips in the multi-step problems or in evaluating.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Applies laws incorrectly, for example multiplying indices in the product law, or cannot combine laws in a sequence.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Justifies each law by expanding and counting or cancelling factors, and explains why a⁰ = 1 using both the quotient law and arithmetic.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Justifies some laws by expansion but states others without a reason.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States the laws as rules to memorise with no justification, or believes a⁰ = 0.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Writes clearly, shows each line of working, names the law used at each step, and links the ideas accurately to the Census figure and at least one other Kenyan application.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Working is mostly clear and the laws are named, with a general or partly developed Kenyan link.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Working is missing or hard to follow, laws are not named, and there is no relevant Kenyan link.

No KICD source for Essential Mathematics was available (the KICD Mathematics PDF is the Core Mathematics design), so the learning outcomes, key inquiry questions, competencies, values and PCIs could not be checked and were not changed. For information only, the Core text differs in ways that look suspicious: Core sub-strand 1.2 is 'Indices and Logarithms' (8 lessons); its outcomes are (a) express numbers in index form, (b) derive the laws of indices using factors, (c) apply the laws in different situations; its key inquiry question is 'Why do we use indices and logarithms?'; its values are Responsibility and Respect (here Unity and Responsibility); its PCI is Life Skills (here Social Cohesion); and its core competencies are Learning to learn and Digital literacy (matching here). Please check the Essential Mathematics design.
